title: Legislator's Conviction Can't Be Stayed Only To Avoid Disqualification : Supreme Court
case_name: STATE OF KARNATAKA v. VINAY RAJASHEKHARAPPA KULKARNI AND ANR
ratio: That a legislator's impending disqualification following conviction cannot, by itself, be a ground for staying the conviction…
summary: The Supreme Court has held that that a legislator's impending disqualification following conviction cannot, by itself, be a ground for staying the conviction, observing that such an interpretation would effectively allow every convicted legislator to continue in office and contest subsequent elections by obtaining a stay of conviction.

note.Facts: Karnataka MLA Vinay Kulkarni was convicted on 15 April 2026 for his role in the 2016 murder of BJP leader Yogesh Goudar. The Karnataka High Court stayed his conviction and sentence, fearing disqualification under Section 8(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and suspended sentences of eight convicts.
note.Issue: Whether the prospect of statutory disqualification of a legislator under Section 8(3) RPA 1951 can, by itself, justify a stay of conviction and suspension of sentence.
note.Held: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s orders, holding that the mere possibility of disqualification is not a sufficient ground to stay a conviction; a stay requires a palpable, fatal error in the judgment and an “eminently winnable” case.
note.Principle: A conviction may be stayed only in rare, exceptional cases where the appellant demonstrates a palpable, fatal error on the face of the record that strikes at the foundation of the judgment; the prospect of disqualification under Section 8(3) RPA 1951 is merely a consideration, not a determinative factor.
note.Provisions: Section 8(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951; no other statutes or cases are named in the source.
note.Exam angle: Questions may test the application of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (disqualification provisions) and the high threshold for staying a conviction—focus on the “palpable mistake” test and its relevance to legislative disqualification.

title: NCR Homeloan Subvention Scam : Supreme Court Directs Banks To Grant Prosecution Sanction Against Officers
summary: A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana was dealing with a batch of pleas concerning subvention schemes in India, where it earlier suspected an "unholy nexus" between builders and banks resulting in distress for homebuyers.

note.Facts: Homebuyers in Delhi-NCR invested in tripartite subvention schemes where builders promised to pay EMIs until possession; developers defaulted, banks and NBFCs pursued buyers for EMIs and disbursed loans directly to builders, breaching RBI guidelines.
note.Issue: Whether banks and NBFCs must grant unconditional sanction for prosecution of their officers in the corruption cases arising from the subvention scam.
note.Held: The Supreme Court directed the concerned banks and NBFCs (HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Sammaan Capital, PNB Housing Finance) to issue unconditional prosecution sanctions within one week, failing which their CMDs and Chairpersons must appear and show cause.
note.Principle: Courts may compel financial institutions to grant unconditional sanction for prosecution of their officers when FIRs are registered pursuant to judicial orders, to prevent coercive recovery actions against homebuyers.
note.Provisions: Not stated (the source does not cite specific statutes or sections).
note.Exam angle: Likely framed under the Banking Regulation Act / RBI guidelines and criminal procedure – focus on the requirement of sanction for prosecution of bank officers and the court’s power to direct unconditional sanction in cases of judicially-ordered FIRs.

title: How reasonable is ‘reasonable’? - Supreme Court Observer
summary: Home > Analysis > How reasonable is ‘reasonable’? This Constitution Day, we revisit the making of Article 19 and the constitutional limits on the State’s power to restrict protests. “Life would be meaningless”, wrote Hansa Mehta in May 1945, if the individual did not enjoy, among other freedoms, the right to speak, associate and convene.

note.Facts: The Supreme Court examined State restrictions on public protests, including the use of Section 144, CPC 1973, and the denial of bail to alleged conspirators under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, in the context of repeated demonstrations such as the 2011 Baba Ramdev agitation and the 2020 Delhi riots.
note.Held: The Court held that any restriction on the freedom of speech, expression or peaceful assembly must pass the test of proportionality; mere blanket prohibitions or repetitive orders amount to an abuse of power and are unconstitutional.
note.Principle: Restrictions on fundamental freedoms under Article 19 must be *reasonable* and *proportionate* to the intended public-order objective; otherwise they violate the Constitution.
note.Provisions: State of Bihar* (1962), *Ramlila Maidan* (2012), *Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India* (2020), *Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India* (2018).
note.Exam angle: Questions may test the *Reasonableness Test* under Article 19(1) – ask candidates to list the ingredients of proportionality (legitimate aim, rational nexus, balance of convenience) and to apply them to statutory restrictions such as Section 144 or UAPA-based detentions.

title: Supreme Court Quashes Bihar Govt's Remission Granted To Ex-MP Anand Mohan In IAS Officer's Murder Case
summary: The Court directed Anand Mohan to surrender within a month, after finding that the 2023 amendment made to the remission policy, whereby the bar on persons sentenced to life for the murder of public servants from seeking remission was removed.

note.Facts: Former MP Anand Mohan, sentenced to life for the 1994 mob-lynching murder of IAS Officer G Krishnaiah, was released in April 2023 after the Bihar Government amended its remission policy to remove the bar on remission for murder of public servants.
note.Issue: Whether the 2023 amendment to Bihar’s remission policy, allowing persons sentenced to life for murdering a public servant to seek remission, is constitutionally valid.
note.Held: The Supreme Court set aside the remission, declared the amendment unconstitutional, and ordered Anand Mohan to surrender within a month.
note.Principle: An amendment that removes a statutory bar on remission for murder of public servants, without a rational and legitimate public purpose, violates Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution; the victim must be heard before remission is granted, though the victim’s objection is not a veto.
note.Provisions: Articles 14, 21 of the Constitution; Rule 481(1)(a) of the Bihar Prison Manual, 2012 (as amended); the Bihar remission policy (pre-amendment bar of 20 years for murder of public servants).
note.Exam angle: Constitutional law – test of equality and due-process clauses (Arts 14, 21) in the context of remission statutes; could be asked on the validity of legislative/amendatory actions affecting punishment, or on procedural safeguards (hearing the victim) in remission decisions.
